sentences.text: The holotype specimen consists of a partial skeleton containing numerous vertebrae, ribs, limb bones, and an almost complete articulated left foot.
CT scans performed in 2021 revealed three paleopathologies on the holotype bones, including fractures and a tumor.
A tumor found in the metatarsal bone was likely a malignant bone tumor such as osteosarcoma.
The remains of Bonapartesaurus were excavated by Jaime Powell and collaborators in 1984 and formally described by Powell in 1987.
Fossils were found at the Salitral Moreno site in southern Argentina within the lower member of the Allen Formation, dating to the Late Cretaceous.
Researchers suggest that the identified pathologies caused pain and impaired function but were not the direct cause of death.
Bonapartesaurus is classified within the Hadrosauridae family, specifically following an older definition of Hadrosaurinae that includes non-crested hadrosaurids.
A 2022 revision reclassified Bonapartesaurus into the tribe Kritosaurini as part of a new South American clade including Huallasaurus and Secernosaurus.
Bonapartesaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, between the Campanian and Maastrichtian stages, approximately 70 million years ago in what is now South America.
The animal lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
It is debated whether the material previously attributed to Willinakaqe represents more than one taxon, with researchers concluding that the original diagnostic characteristics were invalid.
Researchers debated the validity of the genus Willinakaqe in 2016, concluding that its fossils likely represented multiple hadrosaurid taxa rather than a single species.

In 2017, Cruzado-Caballero and Powell reclassified the main paratype of Willinakaqe as Bonapartesaurus rionegrensis, rendering Willinakaqe a invalid name due to it being a chimera of different hadrosaurids.
